investment_summary:
Visa's fiscal 2026 shows accelerating growth: net revenue rose 15% to $45.9 billion and value-added services rose 31% [1]. Non-GAAP EPS rose 16% to $13.27, and Visa beat EPS consensus in all four reported quarters [1][3].

Cash generation is solid but stretched. Free cash flow of $22.1 billion did not cover $25.6 billion of buybacks and dividends, so cash fell to $12.9 billion [1][2].

Valuation is demanding. Consensus, dated 2026-11-25 and therefore after the 10-K, expects 11.3% revenue growth in FY2027 and a forward P/E of 27.7x [3]. The reverse DCF implies 13.2% annual revenue growth for ten years, above both consensus and the 12.0% three-year CAGR. On that path the implied return is 6.7% against an 8.8% WACC, so the price requires growth above consensus for a decade [2][3]. Main risks are fee regulation and $15.9 billion of interchange at issue in litigation [1].
key_takeaways: Value-added services should keep lifting growth: VAS rose 31% to $14.2 billion, outpacing the 15% total revenue gain [1].
Shareholder returns will have to slow: $25.6 billion of buybacks and dividends exceeded $22.1 billion of free cash flow [1][2].
The price already assumes more than consensus: the reverse DCF needs 13.2% annual growth versus 11.3% consensus for FY2027 [2][3].
Litigation and fee regulation are the key downside: $15.9 billion of interchange is at issue in U.S. covered litigation [1].
business_overview:
Visa Inc. is a global payments technology company. Through VisaNet, it provides authorization, clearing and settlement among consumers, financial institutions and sellers in more than 200 countries and territories [1]. Visa is not a bank: it does not issue cards or extend credit, and it earns fees on payment volume and services. In fiscal 2026 (year ended September 30, 2026), net revenue rose 15% to $45.9 billion from $40.0 billion, and net income rose 17% to $23.5 billion [1]. The company reports three business lines: consumer payments, Commercial and Money Movement Solutions (CMS), and value-added services (VAS) [1].

Growth is increasingly led by services beyond the core transaction. VAS revenue rose 31% to $14.2 billion from $10.9 billion [1]. Data processing revenue rose 17% to $23.4 billion, and service revenue rose 14% to $19.9 billion [1]. Visa processed 281.3 billion transactions in the year, up 9%, and Visa Direct handled more than 15 billion transactions for more than 800 clients [1]. The filing does not disclose VAS margins, so the profit contribution of these services cannot be isolated.

Capital allocation and portfolio moves were active. Visa acquired Prisma and Newpay in Argentina for $1.5 billion in cash in February 2026, and in August 2026 agreed to buy BioCatch for $2.4 billion, subject to regulatory approval [1]. It returned $20.5 billion through buybacks, paid $5.1 billion in dividends, and raised its quarterly dividend 16% to $0.78 [1][2]. At the 2026-11-05 closing price of $435.76, the shares sat close to their 52-week high of $435.95 [2]. Consensus, dated 2026-11-25, rated the stock buy with a $453.22 average target [3].
market_position:
Visa's end markets are global and weighted toward international flows. International markets produced $28.5 billion, or 62% of fiscal 2026 net revenue, up 17%, while the U.S. produced $17.4 billion (38%), up 11% [1]. International nominal payments volume grew 12% and U.S. volume grew 8% in the twelve months to June 2026 [1]. Cross-border volume excluding intra-Europe rose 15% [1]. This geographic mix diversifies revenue, but it also exposes Visa to currency, travel and geopolitical swings that the filing flags directly [1].

Visa is the scale leader among the card networks the filing compares. In calendar 2025, its total volume was the largest of the five networks cited, ahead of Mastercard, American Express, Diners Club/Discover and JCB [1]. The 10-K does not name major clients, so client concentration cannot be fully assessed, although it states that a significant portion of net revenue comes from the largest clients [1]. Its reach is broad, with more than 14,000 financial institution clients and over 400 million seller locations [1].

Competition is shifting toward new rails. The filing names closed-loop networks such as American Express and Discover, alternative systems such as Alipay and WeChat Pay, fintechs, and government-backed real-time payment networks [1]. More than 225 stablecoin-linked card programs exist [1]. We classify Visa as a market leader: it holds the largest share of volume and is defending it against new rails, rather than gaining share from a weaker position.
operating_results:
Fiscal 2026 net revenue rose 15% to $45.9 billion from $40.0 billion, led by data processing revenue (up 17%) and service revenue (up 14%) [1]. Cost of revenue rose about 15% to $9.0 billion, so gross margin held at 80.4% [1][4]. Operating expenses rose 11% to $17.8 billion, including $563 million of severance tied to efficiency actions. Marketing rose 37%, partly from FIFA World Cup 2026 and Milano Cortina sponsorships [1]. The litigation provision fell to $1.8 billion from $2.6 billion, lifting GAAP operating income about 12% to $29.9 billion and the GAAP operating margin to 61.2% from 60.0% [1].

Net income rose 17% to $23.5 billion, a net margin of 51.2% against 50.1% [1]. Diluted GAAP EPS rose 21% to $12.32, helped by a 4% fall in diluted shares after $20.5 billion of buybacks [1]. That GAAP figure includes a $314 million deferred tax benefit that Visa excludes from non-GAAP results. On that basis, net income rose 12% to $25.3 billion and EPS rose 16% to $13.27 [1]. Part of the GAAP margin gain therefore reflects lower litigation accruals rather than operating leverage alone [1].

Consensus expects revenue of $51.1 billion in FY2027, growth of 11.3%, and EPS of $15.03 [3]. The current-year EPS consensus is up 0.2% over 90 days, with 23 analysts raising estimates against 10 cutting in the last 30 days [3]. Visa beat EPS estimates in all four reported quarters, by 0.9% to 6.8%, with the largest beat in the quarter ended March 31, 2026 [3]. Consensus data is dated 2026-11-25, after the 10-K.
risk_assessment:
Regulation is the largest risk to the fee base. The filing describes a U.S. Federal Reserve cap on debit interchange, a proposed further cut, conflicting federal court decisions that could lower the debit cap further, and the Credit Card Competition Act, which has been reintroduced [1]. In Europe, the Interchange Fee Regulation caps consumer credit and debit rates, and a 2019 settlement limiting certain cross-border rates runs through 2029 [1]. Because interchange drives payments volume, these caps could reduce net revenue.

Competition and disintermediation form the second risk. Closed-loop networks, alternative systems, stablecoins under the GENIUS Act, and real-time government networks could move flows away from Visa, particularly in cross-border and B2B payments [1]. Client concentration adds to this, since the largest clients can terminate on short notice [1]. The filing also flags pressure on incentives, which could moderate growth [1].

Settlement, cyber and litigation exposure carries the most severe consequences. Visa indemnifies issuers and acquirers for settlement losses, and under Brazilian rules it may absorb some settlement losses, with exposure expected to rise once approved [1]. The filing warns that a failure of its retrospective responsibility plans could cause the company to become insolvent, and it cites $15.9 billion of interchange at issue in unresolved U.S. covered litigation [1]. Fiscal 2026 free cash flow of $22.1 billion covers that exposure only in part, and the balance sheet is weighted toward intangibles: goodwill and intangibles total $48.2 billion, so tangible book value is negative at -$12.6 billion [1][2]. Investors should weigh these exposures alongside a high valuation, with the stock at about 27.7x forward earnings [3].
competitors_analysis:
Against Mastercard (MA), the closest business model and a similar card network, Visa leads on scale and gross margin. Visa's gross margin was 80.4% in 2025 against Mastercard's 77.9%, and its revenue growth was 14.8% in 2026 [2][4]. Mastercard earns a higher return on invested capital, at 58.2% against Visa's 33.0% in 2025, and it grew faster in 2025 [2][4]. The EBITDA margin lead also narrowed sharply, from about 11.6 points in 2024 to 2.7 points in 2025 [4].

American Express (AXP) is a closed-loop competitor the filing names directly [1]. Its revenue is larger, at $72.2 billion in 2025 against Visa's $40.0 billion, but its growth is slower at 9.5% against Visa's 11.3% in 2025 [4]. The data does not provide gross margin or EBITDA for AXP, so the comparison relies on revenue growth and cash conversion alone [4]. Visa's FCF conversion of 0.94 in 2026 trails AXP's 1.2 to 2.5 range in prior years [4].

PayPal (PYPL) represents the digital-wallet and alternative rails the filing warns about [1]. Its gross margin of about 46% is far below Visa's 80.4%, and its EBITDA margin of about 23% is well below Visa's 65.0% in 2025 [4]. Its growth slowed each year, to 4.3% in 2025 against Visa's 11.3% [4]. On valuation, Visa's EV/EBITDA of 22.5 sits well above PayPal's 7.2, and near Mastercard's 25.4 in 2025 [4]. Visa's premium is supported by margins and growth, but the weaker FCF conversion and the 2025 margin decline are points to watch [4].

investment_theses.thesis: Value-added services will keep Visa's revenue growth near or above 11% even if transaction growth slows.
investment_theses.evidence: VAS revenue rose 31% to $14.2 billion, while processed transactions rose 9% and total net revenue rose 15% [1]. Consensus expects 11.3% revenue growth in FY2027 [3].
investment_theses.signpost: VAS revenue growth stays in double digits in each quarter reported through June 30, 2027.
investment_theses.invalidation: VAS growth below 15% for two consecutive quarters, or FY2027 net revenue growth below 10%.

investment_theses.thesis: Buybacks will be trimmed toward free cash flow, because shareholder returns currently exceed the cash generated.
investment_theses.evidence: Buybacks of $20.5 billion and dividends of $5.1 billion exceeded free cash flow of $22.1 billion; cash fell to $12.9 billion from $17.2 billion [1][2].
investment_theses.signpost: FY2027 buybacks at or below $22 billion, reported in the FY2027 10-K (about November 2027).
investment_theses.invalidation: Buybacks above $25 billion funded by new debt, or cash below $10 billion at September 30, 2027.

investment_theses.thesis: At the current price, returns will lag the cost of capital unless Visa beats consensus growth for a decade.
investment_theses.evidence: The reverse DCF implies 13.2% growth against 11.3% FY2027 consensus; implied return is 6.7% versus an 8.8% WACC [2][3].
investment_theses.signpost: FY2027 revenue at or above the $51.1 billion consensus, reported in the November 2027 10-K.
investment_theses.invalidation: FY2027 revenue growth below 10%, or consensus FY2027 EPS cut below $14.67, the low end of the range [3].

investment_theses.thesis: Litigation and fee regulation will not dent Visa's volume in FY2027.
investment_theses.evidence: The litigation provision fell to $1.8 billion from $2.6 billion, but $15.9 billion of interchange remains at issue in U.S. covered litigation [1].
investment_theses.signpost: Litigation provision at or below $2.0 billion in FY2027, and no enacted U.S. debit interchange cap by September 30, 2027.
investment_theses.invalidation: Litigation provision above $2.6 billion, or a U.S. debit cap enacted that cuts net revenue growth below 10%.
